'''''Melia azedarach''''', commonly known as the '''chinaberry tree''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 15 December 2017 }}</ref> '''pride of India''',<ref>{{cite book |author=Nelson |first=Gil |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vNMnsHiDkOkC&pg=PA213 |title=The Shrubs and Woody Vines of Florida – A Reference and Field Guide |publisher=Pineapple Press Inc |year=1996 |isbn=978-1-56164-110-9 |pages=213 |chapter=Meliaceae - Mahogany Family }}</ref> '''bead-tree''', '''Cape lilac''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''syringa berrytree''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''Persian lilac''',<ref name=GRIN/>  '''Indian lilac''', or '''white cedar''',<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2008/melia-azedarach.html |title=Melia azedarach |website=Australian National Botanic Gardens |date=2015 |publisher=Australian Government |access-date=30 November 2019 |archive-date=26 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210226210947/http://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2008/melia-azedarach.html |url-status=live }}</ref> is a species of [[deciduous]] tree in the [[mahogany]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Meliaceae]], that is native to [[Indomalayan realm|Indomalaya]] and [[Australasian realm|Australasia]].<ref name="Mabberley1984">{{Cite journal |last1=Mabberley |first1=David J. |date=5 September 1984 |title=A Monograph of ''Melia'' in Asia and the Pacific: The history of White Cedar and Persian Lilac |url=http://www.sbg.org.sg/images/4_4_Research_Gardens_Bulletin/4_4_37_1_pdf_Vol_37_Part_1_1984/4.4.37.1.02_y1984_V37P1_GBS_pg.49.pdf |journal=The Gardens' Bulletin Singapore |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=49–64 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171216034521/https://www.sbg.org.sg/images/4_4_Research_Gardens_Bulletin/4_4_37_1_pdf_Vol_37_Part_1_1984/4.4.37.1.02_y1984_V37P1_GBS_pg.49.pdf |archive-date=16 December 2017 |access-date=18 June 2014 }}</ref>

== Description ==

The fully grown tree has a rounded crown, and commonly measures {{convert|7|–|12|m|abbr=off|-1}} tall, exceptionally {{convert|45|m|-1|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Floyd |first=A. G. |title=Rainforest Trees of Mainland South-eastern Australia |publisher=Inkata Press |year=1989 |isbn=978-0-909605-57-5 |pages=204 }}</ref>

The [[leaves]] are up to {{convert|50|cm|abbr=off}} long, alternate, long-petioled, two or three times compound (odd-pinnate); the [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]] are dark green above and lighter green below, with serrate margins.

The [[flower]]s are small and fragrant, with five pale purple or lilac petals, growing in clusters.

The fruit is a [[drupe]], marble-sized, light yellow at maturity, hanging on the tree all winter, and gradually becoming wrinkled and almost white.

''Melia azedarach'' has a short lifespan, averaging about 20 years.<ref>{{cite web |title=Melia azedarach |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2008/melia-azedarach.html |website=Growing Native Plants |access-date=16 November 2024 }}</ref>

=== Chemistry ===
Italo et al. 2009 and Safithri and Sari 2016 report [[flavonoid]]s and [[phenol]]s found in ''M. azedarach''.<ref name="Ozturk-2018">{{cite book |title=Plant and human health |publisher=[[Springer Publishing|Springer]] |year=2018 |isbn=978-3-319-93997-1 |editor-last1=Öztürk |editor-first1=Munir |publication-place=[[Cham, Switzerland]] |oclc=1055656284 |editor-last2=Hakeem |editor-first2=Khalid Rehman}} {{ISBN|978-3-030-06768-7}}.</ref>{{rp|490}}

== Etymology ==
The genus name ''Melia'' is derived from {{wikt-lang|grc|μελία}} ({{grc-transl|μελία}}), the Greek word used by [[Theophrastus]] (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) for ''[[Fraxinus ornus]]'',<ref>{{Cite book |title=Abrégé du dictionnaire grec français |last=Bailly |first=Anatole |date=1 January 1981 |publisher=Hachette |isbn=2-01-003528-3 |location=Paris |oclc=461974285 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.tabularium.be/bailly/ |title=Greek-french dictionary online |last=Bailly |first=Anatole |website=www.tabularium.be |access-date=18 October 2018 |archive-date=5 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161005113310/http://www.tabularium.be/bailly/ |url-status=live }}</ref> which has similar [[Leaf|leaves]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Quattrocchi |first=Umberto |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kaN-hLL-3qEC |title=CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names |publisher=CRC Press |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8493-2677-6 |volume=3 M-Q |pages=1650–1651 |access-date=3 September 2020 |archive-date=11 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811015439/https://books.google.com/books?id=kaN-hLL-3qEC |url-status=live }}</ref> The species name ''azedarach'' is from the {{Langx|fr|azédarac}}, which in turn is from the {{Langx|fa|آزاددرخت|4=free- or noble tree}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=azedarach |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/azedarach |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250710142040/https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/azedarach |archive-date=10 July 2025 |access-date=10 July 2025 |website=[[Merriam-Webster]] }}</ref>

''Melia azedarach'' should not be confused with the ''[[Azadirachta]]'' trees, which are in the same family, but a different genus.

Its common name derives from the fact that its range includes China and it produces berries.<ref>{{cite web |title=Melia azedarach |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/melia-azedarach/ |website=NC State Extension |publisher=North Carolina State University |access-date=26 February 2025 }}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:1A-M.azedarach-003.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the flowers]]
[[File:Melia azedarach kz02.jpg|thumb|Close-up of a cluster of ripe fruits]]
[[File:Indian Grey Hornbill (Ocyceros birostris) eating Bakain (Melia Azadirachta) berries at Roorkee, Uttarakhand W IMG 9016.jpg|thumb|[[Indian grey hornbill]] eating ''Melia azedarach'' fruit in [[Uttarakhand]], India.]]
[[File:Egyptian Rousette, 2293. Sk., Muratpaşa, Анталья ил, TR imported from iNaturalist photo 187450355.jpg|thumb|[[Egyptian fruit bat|Egyptian rousette]] feeding on chinaberries, in Turkey]]
Some hummingbirds like the [[sapphire-spangled emerald]] (''Amazilia lactea''), [[glittering-bellied emerald]] (''Chlorostilbon lucidus'') and [[planalto hermit]] (''Phaethornis pretrei'') have been recorded as feeding on and pollinating the flowers, though only opportunistically.<ref>Baza Mendonça & dos Anjos (2005){{page needed|date=January 2024 }}</ref>{{page needed|date=January 2024}} Bees and butterflies do not use the flower (or the nectar), so it serves no pollinator benefit in places where it has been introduced such as the United States.<ref name="Texas"/>

Pests such as cape lilac tree caterpillars (''[[Leptocneria reducta]]'') have been known to severely defoliate the tree and cause large-scale damage to stands of the trees in Australia.<ref name=ANBG/> The [[fungal]] plant pathogen ''[[Pseudocercospora subsessilis]]'' is found on the leaves of the tree,<ref>{{cite web |title=Species Fungorum - Names Record |url=https://www.speciesfungorum.org/Names/NamesRecord.asp?RecordID=175934 |website=www.speciesfungorum.org |access-date=17 September 2023 }}</ref> causing leaf spots.<ref name=Seo2013>{{cite journal |last1=Seo |first1=S.T. |last2=Shin |first2=C.H. |last3=Park |first3=J.H. |last4=Shin |first4=H.D. |title=First report of leaf spot caused by ''Pseudocercospora subsessilis'' on ''Melia azedarach'' in Korea. |journal=Plant Disease |date=2013 |volume=97 |issue=7 |page=993 |doi=10.1094/PDIS-10-12-1004-PDN |pmid=30722579 |bibcode=2013PlDis..97..993S }}</ref>

A mature Chinaberry tree can survive versatile environments, withstanding temperatures as low as -5˚C and as high as 39˚C[https://sites.redlands.edu/trees/species-accounts/chinaberry/]. According to the USDA, the tree exists as far north as New York.<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=MEAZ  (Distribution data)]</ref>

==Uses==
The plant was introduced around 1830 as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] in the United States (South Carolina and Georgia) and widely planted in the southern states, where its leaves were used to repel insects and its berries were used for homemade whiskey and soap.<ref>[[Walter L. Fleming]], ''Civil War and Reconstruction in Alabama'', [https://archive.org/details/civilwarreconstr00flemuoft/page/234/mode/1up?view=theater p.234] (New York: [[Columbia University Press]], 1905) (retrieved 10 November 2024).</ref> The plant was introduced into Hawaii in 1840.<ref name="Texas"/> It is considered an [[invasive species]] in Texas,<ref name="Texas">{{cite web |title=CHINABERRY TREE details |url=http://www.tsusinvasives.org/home/database/melia-azedarach |website=www.tsusinvasives.org |access-date=18 September 2023 }}</ref> Oklahoma, and as far north as Virginia.<ref>Langeland & Burks</ref> U.S. [[Nursery (horticulture)|nurseries]] continue to sell the trees, however, and the seeds are also widely available. It has become naturalized in tropical and warm temperate regions of [[the Americas]] and is intentionally planted in similar climates around the world. It is an ornamental tree in the southern part of Korea.<ref name=Seo2013/>

In Australia, white cedar is commonly planted in parks, public gardens, stream banks, and along footpaths or roadsides.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Batcher |first1=M.S. |title=Element of Stewardship Abstract for ''Melia azedarach'' |date=2008 |publisher=The Nature Conservancy }}</ref> Particularly in the suburbs of [[Melbourne]], the tree is used in [[nature strip]] plantings by local councils for amenity reasons as well as environmental, social, and economic benefits.<ref>{{cite web |title=Street and Park Tree Management Strategy |url=https://www.yourkingstonyoursay.com.au/31453/documents/66682 |website=City of Kingston |access-date=28 November 2019 |archive-date=28 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191128110312/https://www.yourkingstonyoursay.com.au/31453/documents/66682 |url-status=live }}</ref> The fragrant lilac flowers and yellow fruits make it an appealing ornamental tree.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Elliot |first1=W.R. |last2=Jones |first2=D.L. |title=Encyclopedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Horticulture |date=1993 |publisher=Thomas C. Lothian Pty Ltd |location=Melbourne. |edition=6 }}</ref> The hard seeds of the plant are also used in arts and crafts, such as making beads for [[rosaries]].
It has been noted to be a prolific seed producer and in Australia has naturalized outside its native range and is especially invasive in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, and is considered a weed in the latter state and in New Zealand since it has the ability to colonise an area (via bird-dropped seed) if left unchecked.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hussey |first1=B.M.J. |last2=Keighery |first2=G.J. |last3=Dodd |first3=J. |last4=Lloyd |first4=S.G. |last5=Cousens |first5=R.D. |title=Western Weeds: a guide to the weeds of Western Australia . |date=1997 |publisher=Plant Protection Society of Western Australia (Inc.) }}</ref><ref name=ANBG>{{cite web |first=Toh Ming |last=Sheng |title=''Melia azedarach'' - Growing Native Plants |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2008/melia-azedarach.html |website=www.anbg.gov.au |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=18 September 2023 |language=en }}</ref>

In Kenya the trees have been grown by farmers and used as [[fodder]] for livestock. The leaves can be fed to cattle to improve milk yields and farm incomes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2010 |title=Fodder trees for more milk and income |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/57a08b0be5274a27b200090b/DFID_impact_case_study_Fodder_trees_FINAL_1_.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=14 July 2021 |archive-date=25 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190725144031/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/57a08b0be5274a27b200090b/DFID_impact_case_study_Fodder_trees_FINAL_1_.pdf }}</ref> The taste is not as bitter as that of the leaves of [[neem]] (''Azadirachta indica'').

{{original research|section|date=January 2024}}
[[File:Melia azedarach00.jpg|thumb|''Melia azedarach'' plank]]
The main utility of chinaberry is its timber, which is of medium density and ranges in colour from light brown to dark red. In appearance it is readily confused with the unrelated Burmese teak (''[[Tectona grandis]]''). ''Melia azedarach'', in keeping with other members of the family [[Meliaceae]], has a timber of high quality, but in comparison to many almost-[[extinct]] species of [[mahogany]], it is under-utilised. [[Wood drying|Seasoning]] is relatively simple — planks dry without cracking or [[wood warping|warping]] and are resistant to fungal infection.

The tough, five-grooved seeds were once widely used for making [[rosaries]] and other products requiring [[bead]]s, though in the modern era the seeds have often been replaced by plastics. The cut branches with mature fruit are sold commercially to the florist and landscaping trade, particularly as a component for outdoor holiday decor. The fruits may persist for some time prior to shattering off the stem or discoloring, which occurs rapidly after a relatively short time in subfreezing weather.

''M. azedarach'' leaves and fruits have been used as a natural [[insecticide]] to keep with [[stored food]], but must not be eaten as they are highly poisonous.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=128 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364 }}</ref> Placing the berries in, for example, drying apples and keeping the fruit turned in the sun without damaging any of the chinaberry skin will prevent insect larvae from growing in the dried apples.{{Citation needed|date=October 2018}} A mature tree can yield approximately 15 kilograms of fruit annually.[https://doi.org/10.1186/1756-3305-4-72]

The species has also been used as a traditional herbal medicine. A diluted [[infusion]] of the leaves has been used in the past to induce [[uterus|uterine]] relaxation.{{Citation needed|date=October 2018}} The tree's [[limonoid]] compounds have useful anticancer and antimalarial effects.[https://books.google.com/books?id=22W8EAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Melia+azedarach%22+human+poisonous&pg=PA118]

== Toxicity ==
The fruits have evolved to be eaten by animals, which eat the flesh surrounding the hard [[endocarp]] or ingest the entire fruit and later [[Defecation|vent]] the endocarp. If the endocarp is crushed or damaged during ingestion or digestion, the animal will be exposed to the toxins within the seed. The processes of [[mastication]] and digestion, and the degree of immunity to the particular toxins, vary widely between species, and there is accordingly great variation in clinical symptoms following ingestion.<ref name="Watt-Brandwijk-1962">{{cite book |last1=Watt |first1=John Mitchell |title=The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern Africa |last2=Breyer-Brandwijk |first2=Maria Gerdina |year=1962 |asin=B0058WI2ZU}} [[AGRIS]] id [http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=US201300681257 US201300681257]. [[Invasive Species Compendium|CABI ISC]] [http://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/19620605093 19620605093].</ref>

The fruits are poisonous or narcotic to humans<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=1994 |isbn=0-394-50761-4 |edition=Chanticleer Press |page=517 |orig-date=1980 }}</ref> if eaten in large quantities.<ref>Russell ''et al.'' (1997){{page needed|date=January 2024 }}</ref>{{page needed|date=January 2024}} According to Chinese medical literature, human poisoning can occur if 6–9 fruits, 30–40 seeds, or 400 grams of bark are eaten. The toxins include [[neurotoxin]]s and unidentified resins, found mainly in the fruits.{{fact|date=January 2024}} The first symptoms of poisoning appear a few hours after ingestion. They may include loss of appetite, vomiting, constipation or diarrhea, bloody faeces, stomach pain, pulmonary congestion, cardiac arrest, rigidity, lack of coordination and general weakness. Death may take place after about 24 hours.{{fact|date=January 2024}} As in its relatives, [[tetranortriterpenoid]]s constitute an important toxic principle. These are chemically related to [[azadirachtin]], the primary [[insecticide|insecticidal]] compound in the commercially important [[neem oil]]. These compounds are probably related to the wood and seed's resistance to pest infestation, and maybe to the unattractiveness of the flowers to animals.{{Citation needed|date=October 2018}} The plant is toxic to cats.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Toxic and Non-Toxic Plant List - Cats |url=https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/cats-plant-list |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518175146/https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/cats-plant-list |archive-date=18 May 2021 |access-date=23 May 2021 |website=ASPCA }}</ref>

However, these toxins are not harmful to many species of bird, who gorge themselves on the fruit, eventually reaching a "drunken" state.{{fact|date=January 2024}} The birds that are able to eat the fruit [[seed dispersal|spread the intact seed]]s in their droppings.
